records.quote:
As a ghost in
good standing, a dues-paying member of Asmodeus Local of the United
Lighthouse Haunters of America, Wully never done nothin' to deserve
this. Evicted!
records.paraphrase: The ghost describes an organized union structure governing ghosts and lighthouses.

records.quote:
Jerry's first impulse was to run like hell. "But I don't believe in
ghosts!"
records.paraphrase: Jerry reacts with fear and denial when confronted with the ghost.

records.quote:
'Twas Junior touched up the
paintings. And 'twas Junior painted Gertrude.
records.paraphrase: Ghostly intervention alters Jerry's paintings and creates new works, changing his artistic fortunes.

records.quote:
Such a delightfully zany
couple! Always joking about a Scottish sea captain who lives in the
attic and is married to an Indian princess.
records.paraphrase: The community treats as a joke what the narrative has presented as real, contrasting outside perception with story facts.

records.quote:
She could materialize if she wanted
to. She doesn't want to.
records.paraphrase: Rule explaining that ghostly materialization is a controllable act.

records.quote: Of course you do. If you didn't, you couldn't have seen me.
records.paraphrase: The ghost states a rule that belief is a precondition for perceiving him.

records.quote:
One end of the necktie became longer and longer as its opposite
end shortened. With a final but quiet jerk, the necktie came free,
hesitated for a moment opposite Wesley's belt buckle, then folded
itself neatly and floated away.
records.paraphrase: A ghost supernaturally manipulates Wesley's necktie during the confrontation.

records.quote:
Meanwhile, what collector
hasn't heard of J. Masterson-Junior, whose canvases are lauded for
their "other world" quality?
records.paraphrase: The ghostly help leads to lasting fame and a body of celebrated work.

records.quote: "I think I'm losing my mind," she said.
records.paraphrase: Heather reacts with disorientation on witnessing the ghosts.

records.quote: Celeste only materializes once every seven years.
records.paraphrase: A stated periodicity governing when a particular spirit becomes visible.

records.quote:
No matter what you
think, you couldn't see him if you didn't believe.
records.paraphrase: Restatement of the rule that perceiving ghosts requires belief.

records.quote: I'm not eligible. Employees, relatives etc.
records.paraphrase: The ghost explains bureaucratic-style eligibility rules limiting who can benefit from good luck.

records.quote:
Selecting
one, the stranger said, "Thank you, Junior. You can go now." He turned,
lit Jerry's cigarette and his own.
records.paraphrase: A supernatural helper produces floating coals, introducing the presence of ghosts into the mundane setting.

candidate.paraphrase: A spirit explains the anatomy of a fantastical creature whose left legs are shorter, fitted with prosthetics.

criteria.rationale: The story offers only supernatural folklore rules (belief enables perception, seven-year materialization cycles) framed as whimsical ghost-lore, not scientific facts, theories, discoveries, natural processes, or speculative sciences. These are magical conventions, not science.

No device, technique, engineered system, or invention materially affects the setting or outcome. Ordinary items (razor, scissors, paints, a necktie) are mundane contemporary objects; the plot turns on ghostly magic, not on any invention.
The story is set in a contemporary small town with no speculative future, remote past, or temporal displacement. Ghosts referencing their past deaths is not time travel or a remote-past setting.

The consequences developed (artistic fame from ghostly help) flow from a supernatural premise, not from an identifiable scientific, technological, social, or historical premise extrapolated in an SF sense. It is comic fantasy causation rather than reasoned extrapolation.

No observation, hypothesis, testing, measurement, or evidential revision materially drives understanding or action. Characters react with disbelief and wonder; understanding comes from being told the ghost-lore, not from systematic inquiry.

Ghosts and their 'other world' realm constitute nonordinary presences visiting the mundane setting, and the paintings are praised for an 'other world' quality. However, this is a supernatural afterlife rather than another planet, dimension, or cosmic environment in the SF sense, so materiality and interpretation are uncertain.

The only large-scale threat is demolition of a single old lighthouse, a local zoning matter, plus a character's personal financial and romantic troubles. There is no natural, technological, cosmic, biological, or human-caused large-scale disaster.

candidates.description: A systematically organized society of ghosts and supernatural creatures (the United Lighthouse Haunters of America, banshee bands, werewolves, cryptids) governed by bureaucratic rules, union membership, eligibility restrictions, materialization schedules, and a belief-dependent visibility mechanism, coexisting with the mundane human world.

novelty.rationale: The existence of an entire organized ghostly/supernatural social order interwoven with ordinary small-town life is a totalizing difference from the empirical norm, altering the story universe rather than presenting a single isolated haunting.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The story offers a quasi-systematic social organization (unions, dues, eligibility rules, fixed materialization periodicities) that lends internal consistency, but the foundational mechanism is explicitly supernatural (ghosts, belief-conditioned perception, werewolves related to Dracula and Frankenstein). Suvin's cognitive dimension excludes the supernatural; the bureaucratic framing is comedic overlay rather than an immanent nonsupernatural account, so the dimension is genuinely mixed.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The ghostly society drives the entire plot: it saves Jerry's art career, enables his courtship of Heather, disposes of the rival Wesley, and shapes the couple's eventual fame and family life. The narrative logic is wholly determined by the supernatural order.

estrangement.rationale: Readers register the contrast between the community's treatment of the ghosts as a running joke and the narrative's presentation of them as literally real, while characters react with fear and disorientation on encountering the supernatural order.

candidates.description: A rule that supernatural entities can only be perceived by those who believe in them, coupled with voluntary/scheduled materialization.

novelty.rationale: The belief-gated perception rule is an unusual immanent constraint on the storyworld, but it functions as a property of the broader ghost society rather than an independent world-altering novum on its own.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The perception rule rests on an overtly supernatural premise (belief conjuring visibility of ghosts) with no immanent nonsupernatural account; it is a folkloric convention rather than a cognitive one.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The belief rule is a supporting device explaining perception; it does not independently determine the overriding narrative logic, which is driven by the ghosts' interventions.

estrangement.rationale: The insistence that disbelief prevents sight estranges the reader by inverting ordinary assumptions about perception and reality.
